opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Yann and I actually agree on a fair amount, but there's a real difference in where we put language in the story of intelligence.

Yann's position, roughly, is that language is a fairly thin, low-bandwidth layer on top of the real substance of intelligence, which is sensorimotor understanding of the world. He likes to point out that a four-year-old has taken in vastly more data through vision than any language model has seen in text. And he'll say that cats and dogs are smarter than our LLMs in important ways, even though they have no language at all. So for him, if you want to get to human-level intelligence, you build world models from perception, and language is almost an afterthought.

I see it rather differently. I'd agree that a lot of basic intelligence is shared with other animals and doesn't need language. But what makes humans distinctive isn't that we're a bit better at navigating a room than a chimpanzee. It's that around a hundred thousand years ago or so, we got language, and that changed everything. Language isn't just a communication channel. It's a tool for thought, and above all it's how knowledge gets accumulated and transmitted across people and generations. Nearly everything I know about the world, about history, science, places I've never been, I learned through language, not through my own eyes. So language is a very compressed, very high-value encoding of human knowledge. It's not low-bandwidth in the sense that matters; each word carries an enormous amount of abstraction that took humanity a long time to build.

That's also why I think the success of large language models isn't some accident or parlor trick. By learning from text, they're tapping into this distilled record of how humans conceptualize the world. Yann tends to see that as a dead end. I see it as a remarkably good starting point, even if it's not the whole thing.

On symbolic representations, it's a bit subtle, because I'm not an old-fashioned symbolic AI person either. I don't think you hand-build logical rules. But I do think language gives us discrete, compositional, symbolic structure: words, categories, the ability to put concepts together and reason with them. And humans clearly use that as a cognitive scaffold. So I think the right picture is neural systems that learn to use something like symbols, with language being the main way those symbols come into existence and get shared, rather than intelligence being purely about continuous world models learned from video.

So I'd say the disagreement is less "language versus perception" and more about emphasis. Yann thinks language is the icing. I think, for human-level intelligence specifically, it's a big part of the cake.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Yann and I actually agree on a lot more than people assume, but there is a real difference in emphasis, and it comes down to how much we think language is doing in intelligence.

Yann's view, roughly, is that language is a kind of low-bandwidth, lossy serialization of thought. The real action is in world models, in the kind of understanding you get from perceiving and acting in the physical world. A cat doesn't have language, and a cat has a much better model of the physical world than any LLM. So from his perspective, language is a thin layer on top, almost an afterthought, and it's a mistake to think you'll get to intelligence by training on text alone.

I come at this from the opposite direction, partly because I'm a linguist by training. My view is that language isn't just a channel for transmitting thoughts that were fully formed somewhere else. Language is one of the central technologies that made human intelligence what it is. It's how we accumulate knowledge across generations, it's how we do abstract reasoning, and I'd argue it actually shapes a lot of how we think. Humans without language, or raised without exposure to it, don't just lose the ability to communicate. They lose access to a huge amount of cognition. So I'm much less willing to dismiss language as a low-bandwidth side effect.

And I think the empirical record of the last few years is somewhat on my side. The amount of world knowledge, structure, and even reasoning ability you can extract purely from text turned out to be far greater than most people in 2015 would have predicted, and I include myself in that. Text is a highly compressed, highly curated record of what humans know and how they reason about things. That's not nothing. That's arguably the most information-dense training signal we have.

Now, where I do agree with Yann is that text alone is clearly not the whole story. There are things about physical intuition, about continuous dynamics, about grounding, that you're not going to learn well from reading. And I've long been interested in grounded language learning, in connecting language to perception. So I don't think it's language versus world models. I think the interesting question is how they interact.

The other piece is the symbolic question. Yann has sometimes been fairly dismissive of symbols, and historically I was actually on the other side of that fight too, arguing against the old-school symbolic AI people that you should learn representations from data rather than hand-engineer them. But I think the lesson of large language models is that you can have systems that are entirely continuous and learned, and yet they clearly develop something that functions like symbolic structure. Words are discrete symbols, after all, and these models manipulate them quite well. So I'd say we both reject hand-built symbolic systems. I'm just more convinced that discrete, compositional, language-like representations are a feature that emerges from learning and that matters a great deal, rather than something to route around.

astra-6.text:
I think Yann and I agree that intelligence can’t be reduced to language. There’s a great deal we learn through perception and interaction with the world, and language doesn’t capture all of that. But I would give language a much more central role in human intelligence. It’s not simply a channel for reporting thoughts we’ve already formed. It’s also a tool for organizing thought and, crucially, for learning from other people without having to experience everything ourselves.

And I think we need to distinguish symbolic representations from the old idea that you have to build an intelligence entirely out of hand-written rules. Language gives us discrete symbols that we can combine to express new ideas. That’s tremendously powerful. But those symbols can be learned and interpreted by neural networks; there’s no inherent contradiction there.

So where I’d push back is against treating the limitations of language as a reason to discount it. Grounding matters, but so does the extraordinary amount of structure and knowledge that humans have accumulated in language. I see those as complementary sources of intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann and I agree that intelligence can’t be reduced to language. A great deal of human and animal intelligence involves perception, action, and understanding the physical world. Where I’d put a different emphasis is on how much language contributes to the intelligence that humans have.

Language isn’t simply a way of reporting thoughts that we’ve already worked out somewhere else. It gives us a way to organize knowledge, communicate abstractions, and build on what other people have learned. You can learn something through language without having to experience it directly, and that’s an enormously powerful capability.

Similarly, I don’t see neural representations and symbolic representations as mutually exclusive. Words are symbols, and the ability to combine them into structured expressions matters. That doesn’t mean we need to go back to a classical AI system with hand-written rules. We can learn representations and learn how to manipulate them using neural networks.

So I’m sympathetic to Yann’s emphasis on learning from the world beyond text. But I think language provides a much richer source of structure and knowledge than his arguments sometimes suggest. It isn’t the whole of intelligence, but it’s central to explaining what makes human intelligence so powerful.
